text: AWS gives you two layers of network filtering, and they aren't interchangeable. A Security Group attaches to an instance's network interface and filters traffic at the instance level. A Network ACL attaches to a subnet and filters everything in that subnet at once. Most real designs use both — a tight Security Group per instance role, and a NACL mostly left at its permissive default — but mixing up how the two behave causes real outages.

A new Security Group starts with no inbound rules at all, denying everything in, and one default outbound rule allowing everything out to 0.0.0.0/0. You only ever write allow rules — there's no explicit deny and no priority number to reason about, since AWS evaluates every rule and allows traffic matching any of them. Critically, a Security Group is stateful: allow inbound port 443, and the matching response traffic back out is automatically allowed too.

A Network ACL's rules are numbered from 1 to 32766 and evaluated lowest-number first, and the first rule that matches, allow or deny, wins and stops evaluation right there. The --no-egress and --egress flags pick the direction for each entry, because a NACL is stateless: allowing inbound port 443 does nothing for the return traffic. That needs its own separate outbound rule allowing the high ephemeral ports, 1024 through 65535, so the response actually has somewhere to go.

A Security Group never needs an ephemeral-port rule like that — statefulness handles the return traffic for free. A Network ACL always does, which is exactly the detail that breaks a brand-new custom NACL for people coming from Security Groups and assuming return traffic just works the same way.

One more default worth knowing: the default NACL AWS attaches to a VPC's subnets out of the box allows all traffic in both directions, while a custom NACL you create yourself starts by denying everything until you add rules. Both kinds end with an unwritable final rule denying anything nothing else matched. That closes out VPC networking for this chapter — Lesson 17 opens Chapter 5 with the AWS CLI tool behind every single command this chapter just used.
